formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. Doubling means a factor of 2.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A recipe for 4 made for 8 has a factor of 2.

howToSteps.text: Work down the ingredient list and double each amount. Flour, sugar, butter, liquids, and eggs all double in full.

howToSteps.name: Hold back the leavening
howToSteps.text: Baking powder, baking soda, and yeast get about 1 1/2 times, not double. Too much leavening makes bakes rise fast and sink.

howToSteps.name: Season in stages
howToSteps.text: Start salt and strong spices at about 1 1/2 times, then taste and add more. You can always add seasoning. You cannot take it out.

title: Double a Recipe: Scale Any Dish by 2
tutorial: Doubling is the simplest scaling there is, because the factor is 2 and every amount just doubles. A recipe for 4 becomes a recipe for 8. Two cups of flour become 4. One cup of broth becomes 2. Two eggs become 4. There are no awkward fractions, which is why doubling is the best place to start if you are new to scaling.

Almost everything doubles in full: flour, sugar, butter, oil, liquids, vegetables, meat, and eggs. These are the bulk of the recipe, and doubling them is plain multiplication. The scaler above does it one ingredient at a time, so you can work down the list and write the doubled amounts next to the originals before you start cooking.

Leavening is the exception. Baking powder, baking soda, and yeast do not behave like flour. The common rule of thumb is to use about 1 1/2 times the leavening when doubling, not double. Too much baking powder makes a cake shoot up in the oven and then sink in the middle, and it can leave a metallic taste. The same goes for salt and strong spices: start at about 1 1/2 times, then taste and add more.

The pan matters as much as the maths. A doubled cake in the original pan will be twice as deep, take much longer to bake, and may burn on top before the middle sets. Use a pan about twice the area, or bake in two pans, so the batter depth stays the same. Cooking time does not double either. Check for doneness a little early, and trust the toothpick or the thermometer, not the clock.

Doubling is also the easiest way to cook once and eat twice. I double soups, stews, and braises on purpose and freeze the second half, which means the leftovers need storing properly. Cool the extra portion quickly, get it into the fridge or freezer the same day, and label it with the date so you know how long it has been there.
